examples: Only Ana knew the password.
This parking lot is for employees only.
You can only pay by card here.
The ride only takes ten minutes.
Don't worry, it's only a scratch.
She was only sixteen when she moved to New York.
I only found out about it yesterday.
We met only last month, but it feels like years.
I only realized my mistake when I got home.
He ran to the gate, only to find that the flight had closed.
Yelling at him will only make things worse.
Cutting prices would only hurt the brand.
I'd be only too happy to help.
She knew only too well what could go wrong.
The rumors turned out to be only too true.
If only I'd listened to you!
If only we had more time.
If only he would call back.

senses.head: Nothing or no one else; exclusively
examples: Only Ana knew the password.
This parking lot is for employees only.
You can only pay by card here.

senses.head: No more than; just — used to make an amount, a person or a problem sound small or unimportant
examples: The ride only takes ten minutes.
Don't worry, it's only a scratch.
She was only sixteen when she moved to New York.

senses.head: As recently as; not until — with a time word, showing that something happened very recently or later than expected
examples: I only found out about it yesterday.
We met only last month, but it feels like years.
I only realized my mistake when I got home.

senses.head: With the result, often disappointing, that; in the end merely — in only to and before verbs like make and cause
examples: He ran to the gate, only to find that the flight had closed.
Yelling at him will only make things worse.
Cutting prices would only hurt the brand.

senses.head: Very, completely — in only too, often with happy, glad, well or true
examples: I'd be only too happy to help.
She knew only too well what could go wrong.
The rumors turned out to be only too true.

senses.head: Used in if only to express a strong wish or regret about something that is not true
examples: If only I'd listened to you!
If only we had more time.
If only he would call back.

entries.position: before its word — directly before the word or phrase it focuses; in speech usually mid, before the main verb, with stress on the focused word
entries.modifies: nouns, pronouns, numbers, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, phrases and clauses
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Only Ana saw the email (no one else saw it); Ana only saw the email (she saw it but did not read or answer it); Ana saw only the email (nothing else). Fronted only + a time phrase or clause brings inversion: Only then did I understand, not Only then I understood. Not only … but also inverts too when it opens the sentence: Not only did she win, but she also set a record. The adjective (the only child — единственный) and the informal conjunction (I'd go, only I'm busy — но) are other words. Russian только что is just, not only: He has just left. If only takes a past form for a wish about now and the past perfect for regret about the past: If only I knew (если бы я знал), If only I had known (если бы я тогда знал).

entries.meaning: Only; no more than — used to say that something is small, simple or less important than it might seem. ---
examples: I was merely asking a question.
The delay is merely a few days.
This is not merely a technical problem; it's a legal one.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; or before its word
entries.modifies: verbs, nouns and noun phrases, adjectives, prepositional phrases
entries.contrast: Merely means 'no more than', never 'no one else': Only Ana came (nobody else came), not Merely Ana came. It is more formal than just and only. In not merely … but (also) it works like not only … but also: He was not merely late but rude.

examples: It's simply a matter of time.
To register, simply fill out this form.
He didn't mean any harm — he was simply trying to help.
The view from the top was simply amazing.
I simply can't believe she said that.
We simply don't have the money.
The teacher explained the rule simply and clearly.
They live simply, without a car or a TV.
Put more simply, we're out of cash.

senses.head: Just; only; nothing more than
examples: It's simply a matter of time.
To register, simply fill out this form.
He didn't mean any harm — he was simply trying to help.

senses.head: Absolutely; really — used to give strong emphasis, often with a negative
examples: The view from the top was simply amazing.
I simply can't believe she said that.
We simply don't have the money.

senses.head: In a simple, plain or easy-to-understand way
examples: The teacher explained the rule simply and clearly.
They live simply, without a car or a TV.
Put more simply, we're out of cash.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb or before its word in the focusing and degree senses; end in the manner sense
entries.comparison: not gradable — except in the manner sense (more simply, most simply)
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives, nouns and noun phrases, clauses
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: She explained it simply (in an easy, clear way) vs. She simply explained it (she just explained it and did nothing more). Russian просто as a sentence opener (Просто я устал) is not Simply, I'm tired but It's just that I'm tired or I'm just tired.

entries.meaning: Only; entirely — for this reason, or of this kind, and no other. ---
examples: We met purely by chance.
I do it purely for fun.
Their relationship is purely professional.
entries.type: focusing — restricts to one kind, cause or purpose
entries.position: before its word — usually before an adjective or a prepositional phrase
entries.contrast: Russian чисто has two sides: 'purely, only' is purely (purely by chance), but 'cleanly, without mistakes' is not — She speaks English perfectly or without an accent, not She speaks English purely. The fixed pair purely and simply means 'only and for no other reason'.

entries.meaning: Only; not involving anyone or anything else. ---
examples: The driver was solely responsible for the accident.
The money will be used solely for research.
Don't judge a school solely on its test scores.
entries.type: focusing — restricts to one person, cause or purpose
entries.position: before its word — or mid, before the main verb
entries.form: -ly from sole 'single, only': keeps the e — solely, not soly
entries.contrast: Solely means 'with no other person or cause involved', not 'without company': She lives alone (одна), not She lives solely. It is formal; in conversation Americans say only or just. Solely responsible is a common fixed phrase — несёт полную (единоличную) ответственность.

examples: The course is taught exclusively in Spanish.
For three months he ate exclusively plant-based food.
The group focuses exclusively on small businesses.
The singer spoke exclusively to NBC about her divorce.
These sneakers are sold exclusively on our website.
The series streams exclusively on one platform.

senses.head: Only; with nothing or no one else included
examples: The course is taught exclusively in Spanish.
For three months he ate exclusively plant-based food.
The group focuses exclusively on small businesses.

senses.head: Given, sold or shown to one person, company or outlet and no other
examples: The singer spoke exclusively to NBC about her divorce.
These sneakers are sold exclusively on our website.
The series streams exclusively on one platform.

entries.type: focusing — restricts to one person, group or place
entries.position: before its word — or end, after the verb and its object
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian исключительно also means 'extremely' (исключительно красивый), but English exclusively never does — say exceptionally beautiful, not exclusively beautiful. Exclusively only ever means 'and nothing or no one else'.

examples: The storm hit coastal towns, particularly in the South.
I love old movies, particularly westerns.
Traffic is bad, particularly on Friday afternoons.
It was a particularly cold winter.
The food wasn't particularly good.
She seemed particularly happy that morning.
He particularly asked to see you.
I particularly wanted you to hear this.

senses.head: More than others; especially — pointing at one member of a group
examples: The storm hit coastal towns, particularly in the South.
I love old movies, particularly westerns.
Traffic is bad, particularly on Friday afternoons.

senses.head: Very; to an unusual degree — and with not, 'not very'
examples: It was a particularly cold winter.
The food wasn't particularly good.
She seemed particularly happy that morning.

senses.head: Specifically; for a clear, deliberate reason
examples: He particularly asked to see you.
I particularly wanted you to hear this.

entries.position: before its word — before the noun, phrase or adjective it points at; or mid, before the main verb
entries.modifies: nouns and noun phrases, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, clauses
entries.contrast: Particularly goes before the word it focuses; in particular usually goes after it: particularly the South = the South in particular. Not particularly is a softener — 'not very', не особо: I'm not particularly hungry. As with especially, do not open a sentence with it to mean 'most of all': I particularly like jazz, not Particularly I like jazz.

examples: Kids, especially toddlers, need a lot of sleep.
I especially liked the ending.
Drive carefully, especially when it's raining.
This has been an especially hard year.
I'm not especially interested in politics.
The soup was especially good today.
I baked this cake especially for you.
The app was designed especially for older users.

senses.head: Above all; more than others
examples: Kids, especially toddlers, need a lot of sleep.
I especially liked the ending.
Drive carefully, especially when it's raining.

senses.head: Very; to a great degree — and with not, 'not very'
examples: This has been an especially hard year.
I'm not especially interested in politics.
The soup was especially good today.

senses.head: For one particular purpose or person; specially
examples: I baked this cake especially for you.
The app was designed especially for older users.

entries.position: before its word — before the noun, phrase, clause or adjective it points at; or mid, before the main verb
entries.modifies: nouns and noun phrases, prepositional phrases, clauses, adjectives, verbs
entries.form: -ly from the rare adjective especial, related to special
entries.contrast: Do not open a sentence with especially the way Russian opens with особенно: I especially like apples or I like fruit, especially apples, not Especially I like apples. Especially and specially share the 'for a purpose' sense (made especially for you), but only especially means 'above all': I love fruit, especially apples, not specially apples.

entries.meaning: More than anything else; for the most part. ---
examples: The audience was mainly college students.
We moved here mainly because of the schools.
Their customers are mainly in the Midwest.
entries.type: focusing — picks out the largest part or the chief reason
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; or before its word
entries.modifies: verbs, nouns and noun phrases, prepositional phrases, clauses
entries.contrast: Mainly does not usually go at the end: They mainly eat fish or They eat mainly fish, not They eat fish mainly. Mainly and mostly are close, but only mostly means 'most of the time': I mostly work from home is more natural than mainly for habits. Russian в основном as 'on the whole' (В основном всё хорошо) is Overall, everything is fine or Things are mostly fine.

examples: The disease chiefly affects older adults.
The town is known chiefly for its wine.
His novels were written chiefly for young readers.
entries.type: focusing — picks out the largest part or the chief reason
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; or before its word
entries.modifies: verbs, nouns and noun phrases, prepositional phrases, clauses
entries.contrast: Chiefly means 'mainly', not 'as a chief' or 'like a boss'. It is formal and written; in conversation Americans say mainly or mostly.

examples: The app is designed primarily for teachers.
We are primarily a family business.
The problem is primarily a financial one.
entries.type: focusing — picks out the main part, purpose or reason
entries.position: before its word — or mid, before the main verb
entries.modifies: prepositional phrases, clauses, verbs, adjectives, nouns
entries.contrast: Primarily is 'mainly', not 'first in time' as Russian первично or изначально suggests: The house was originally a school, not primarily a school (which means 'mainly a school'). US/UK split: American stress is usually on the second syllable, pry-MAIR-uh-lee; British is PRY-muh-ruh-lee.

examples: She speaks Spanish, and she also speaks French.
The hotel is also close to the beach.
He's not only smart but also very kind.
The rent is too high. Also, it's far from work.
Also, don't forget to lock the back door.

senses.head: In addition; too
examples: She speaks Spanish, and she also speaks French.
The hotel is also close to the beach.
He's not only smart but also very kind.

senses.head: Besides; and another thing — at the start of a sentence, adding a new point
examples: The rent is too high. Also, it's far from work.
Also, don't forget to lock the back door.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; front as a linker
entries.modifies: verbs, whole clauses, nouns and phrases
entries.contrast: Too and also at the end of a negative become either: I don't like it either ('тоже не'), not I don't like it too or I don't like it also. Mid also before a negative is fine when it adds a new point: The room was small, and it also didn't have a window. Russian speakers put also at the end (I like it also); American English puts it mid (I also like it) and uses too at the end. In short replies say Me too, not Me also. Not only … but also splits around the two things joined: She not only sings but also dances.

examples: I don't eat meat, and my husband doesn't either.
If you're not going, I won't go either.
"I've never been to Texas." "I haven't either."
There's a great taco place nearby, and it's not expensive either.
It's a great little car, and it doesn't use much gas either.

senses.head: Also; too — used after a negative statement
examples: I don't eat meat, and my husband doesn't either.
If you're not going, I won't go either.
"I've never been to Texas." "I haven't either."

senses.head: Moreover; for that matter — adding a negative point that makes what was said stronger
examples: There's a great taco place nearby, and it's not expensive either.
It's a great little car, and it doesn't use much gas either.

entries.position: end — at the end of the negative clause
entries.contrast: Either is the negative partner of too: I like it too but I don't like it either, not I don't like it too. In replies, Me neither is standard; Me either is very common in American speech but still marked as informal. The determiner and pronoun (either side, either of them — любой из двух) and the conjunction either … or (или … или) are different words. The pronunciation EYE-thur is also heard in the US.

entries.meaning: Also not — used after a negative statement to say the same is true of another person or thing. ---
examples: "I can't swim." "Neither can I."
She didn't call, and neither did her brother.
"I don't like horror movies." "Me neither."
entries.type: focusing — additive, in negative clauses; also negative
entries.position: front — opens the clause, and the auxiliary comes before the subject; alone after a pronoun in Me neither
entries.modifies: a whole clause, answering or adding to a negative one
entries.contrast: Neither brings inversion: Neither do I, Neither can she, not Neither I do. It already carries the negative, so no not: Neither did he, not Neither didn't he. Neither do I = I don't either; after a positive statement use So do I. The determiner and pronoun (neither answer, neither of them — ни один из двух) and the conjunction neither … nor (ни … ни) are different words. The pronunciation NY-thur is also heard in the US.

examples: Several cities, notably Denver and Austin, have grown fast.
The band had many hits, most notably "Hotel California."
Some groups, notably farmers, opposed the plan.
It was a notably successful year for the company.
The senator was notably absent from the meeting.
Notably, no one on the board objected.
Notably, the report says nothing about costs.

senses.head: Especially; in particular — introducing an important example
examples: Several cities, notably Denver and Austin, have grown fast.
The band had many hits, most notably "Hotel California."
Some groups, notably farmers, opposed the plan.

senses.head: In a way that is remarkable or easy to notice
examples: It was a notably successful year for the company.
The senator was notably absent from the meeting.

senses.head: It is worth pointing out that — commenting on the whole sentence
examples: Notably, no one on the board objected.
Notably, the report says nothing about costs.

entries.position: before its word — before the example it introduces or the adjective it strengthens; front as a comment on the whole sentence
entries.comparison: more/most — mostly in most notably, 'above all'
entries.modifies: nouns and noun phrases, adjectives, whole sentences
entries.contrast: Notably is 'remarkably, in a way worth noting', not 'visibly': something you can see is noticeably — She's noticeably thinner, not notably thinner. Introducing an example, it is close to especially and in particular, and the most common form is most notably.

examples: The program was created specifically for veterans.
These shoes are made specifically for running.
The law specifically targets online lenders.
I specifically told you not to touch my laptop.
The contract specifically says no pets.
We need help with marketing — specifically, social media.
The problem is the software, or, more specifically, the billing module.
What specifically don't you like about it?

senses.head: For one particular purpose, person or group and no other
examples: The program was created specifically for veterans.
These shoes are made specifically for running.
The law specifically targets online lenders.

senses.head: Clearly and directly; in a way that leaves no doubt
examples: I specifically told you not to touch my laptop.
The contract specifically says no pets.

senses.head: To be exact; namely — narrowing down what was just said
examples: We need help with marketing — specifically, social media.
The problem is the software, or, more specifically, the billing module.
What specifically don't you like about it?

entries.position: before its word — or mid, before the main verb; front as more specifically or specifically, 'to be exact'
entries.comparison: more/most — mainly in more specifically, 'to be more exact'
entries.modifies: verbs, prepositional phrases, nouns and noun phrases, whole sentences
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian специфически / специфично means 'peculiarly, in a distinctive way', which English specifically never means — It tastes unusual or It has a distinctive taste, not It tastes specifically. Specifically is about exactness and a clear purpose.

examples: That's exactly what I was going to say.
The twins look exactly alike.
The house is exactly the way we left it.
The bill came to exactly $50.
The meeting starts at exactly nine.
It's been exactly a year since we met.
Follow the instructions exactly.
Copy the code exactly as it appears on the screen.
What exactly do you want from me?
Where exactly did you park the car?
He's not exactly a genius.
"Were you surprised?" "Not exactly."
Five hours in traffic isn't exactly my idea of fun.
"So the real problem is the price?" "Exactly."
"We should have left earlier." "Exactly!"

senses.head: Just; in every way — stressing that something is the very thing meant
examples: That's exactly what I was going to say.
The twins look exactly alike.
The house is exactly the way we left it.

senses.head: No more and no less — with numbers, amounts and times
examples: The bill came to exactly $50.
The meeting starts at exactly nine.
It's been exactly a year since we met.

senses.head: Accurately and carefully, with no mistakes
examples: Follow the instructions exactly.
Copy the code exactly as it appears on the screen.

senses.head: In questions, asking for the precise detail, often with some impatience
examples: What exactly do you want from me?
Where exactly did you park the car?

senses.head: Not really; not at all — in not exactly, used to soften a negative or to be ironic
examples: He's not exactly a genius.
"Were you surprised?" "Not exactly."
Five hours in traffic isn't exactly my idea of fun.

senses.head: Yes, that's right — used alone as a reply to show strong agreement
examples: "So the real problem is the price?" "Exactly."
"We should have left earlier." "Exactly!"

entries.position: before its word — before the word, number or phrase it makes precise; end in the manner sense; alone as a reply
entries.modifies: nouns and noun phrases, numbers and times, wh-words and clauses, adjectives, verbs
entries.contrast: Exactly! agrees with what someone just said (вот именно). Russian Точно! also means 'Oh right, I forgot' — that is Oh, right! or That's right!, not Exactly!. Russian точно as 'definitely' (Он точно придёт) is He'll definitely come, not He'll exactly come. Not exactly is often a polite or ironic 'not at all'.

examples: That's precisely the point I was trying to make.
People came precisely because the event was free.
That's precisely why I called you.
The train left at precisely 7:15.
The box measures precisely two feet across.
The parts must be cut precisely.
She describes the city more precisely than any other writer.
The store opened in early 2020 — or, more precisely, in January.
The problem is the car — more precisely, the brakes.
"So you want us to wait?" "Precisely."
"It's cheaper in the long run." "Precisely."

senses.head: Exactly; just — stressing that something is the very thing or reason meant
examples: That's precisely the point I was trying to make.
People came precisely because the event was free.
That's precisely why I called you.

senses.head: No more and no less — with numbers, amounts and times
examples: The train left at precisely 7:15.
The box measures precisely two feet across.

senses.head: Accurately and with great care over detail
examples: The parts must be cut precisely.
She describes the city more precisely than any other writer.

senses.head: To be exact — in more precisely, correcting or narrowing down what was just said
examples: The store opened in early 2020 — or, more precisely, in January.
The problem is the car — more precisely, the brakes.

senses.head: Yes, that's right — used alone as a reply to show agreement
examples: "So you want us to wait?" "Precisely."
"It's cheaper in the long run." "Precisely."

entries.position: before its word — before the word, number or phrase it makes precise; end in the manner sense; alone as a reply
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense and in more precisely, 'to be more exact'
entries.modifies: nouns and noun phrases, numbers and times, clauses, verbs
entries.contrast: Precisely is a more formal exactly. Or, more precisely, corrects what was just said — точнее, and precisely because stresses that the reason is surprising: I trust him precisely because he disagrees with me. Russian точно meaning 'definitely' is not precisely: I'll definitely be there.

examples: Watch what I do, and then do likewise.
She stood up to leave, and the others did likewise.
He treats everyone with respect and expects to be treated likewise.
Parents should read to their kids every day. Teachers, likewise, should make time to read aloud.
Prices rose in March. Likewise, wages went up slightly.
"It was great to meet you." "Likewise."
"Have a good weekend!" "Likewise!"

senses.head: In the same way; the same thing
examples: Watch what I do, and then do likewise.
She stood up to leave, and the others did likewise.
He treats everyone with respect and expects to be treated likewise.

senses.head: Also; similarly — linking a new point to the one before
examples: Parents should read to their kids every day. Teachers, likewise, should make time to read aloud.
Prices rose in March. Likewise, wages went up slightly.

senses.head: The same to you — used alone as a reply to a polite remark
examples: "It was great to meet you." "Likewise."
"Have a good weekend!" "Likewise!"

entries.position: end — in do likewise; front as a linker; alone as a reply
entries.form: compound of like + -wise 'way', written as one word
entries.contrast: Do likewise means 'do the same thing', not 'do it like someone'. As a reply, Likewise returns a polite wish or feeling (Nice to meet you. — Likewise.), close to Russian взаимно; for a simple fact say Me too: I'm hungry. — Me too, not Likewise.
